title: Five books of prayers
hook: the Psalms are in five books, like the Torah, and cover every feeling

segments.voice: Yesterday, the last psalm, all trumpets and cymbals. Your word was hallelujah, and your line, let everything that has breath. Did a breath go out as thanks? Day four hundred forty-one.

Open a Bible somewhere near the middle and you'll very often land in the Psalms. It's the longest book in it, a hundred and fifty chapters. For the last month this path has walked through it: a tree by the water, a cry of my God, my God, a deer at a dry stream, a sparrow at the altar, a weaned child, exiles by the rivers of Babylon, and yesterday, a crash of cymbals. It can feel like a shuffle playlist. Grief, then joy, then fury, then a lullaby. But it isn't a pile. Someone arranged it. Today, before we leave the Psalms, the shape of the whole book.
screen: `THE MIDDLE OF THE BIBLE.` → `A MONTH IN THE PSALMS.` → `NOT A PILE, A SHAPE.`

segments.voice: The Psalms are divided into five books. Book one runs from Psalm one to forty-one. Book two, forty-two to seventy-two. Book three, seventy-three to eighty-nine. Book four, ninety to one hundred six. Book five, one hundred seven to one hundred fifty. You can see the seams if you look. Each book ends with a blessing, like a door closing. The first one, in the King James Bible: "Blessed be the LORD God of Israel from everlasting, and to everlasting. Amen, and Amen." And at the end of book two there's a surprising little note: "The prayers of David the son of Jesse are ended." Except they aren't. More psalms of David come later. That line is probably left over from an older collection, stitched in whole. The Psalms were gathered over centuries. An old Jewish commentary on the Psalms says that as Moses gave Israel five books of the law, David gave them five books of psalms. Inside, every feeling has a place. The largest group of psalms is lament: complaint, grief, why, how long. Then praise, thanks, pilgrim songs, wisdom, songs for kings. Early Christian writers noticed this. Athanasius, a bishop in Egypt in the fourth century, wrote that the other books of the Bible speak to you, but the Psalms speak for you; you find your own soul in them, as in a mirror. John Calvin later called the book an anatomy of all the parts of the soul. One more note: Greek and Latin Bibles number most psalms one lower, which is why Catholic and Orthodox prayer books can look off by one.
screen: `FIVE BOOKS, FIVE SEAMS` · `THE PRAYERS OF DAVID ARE ENDED` · `LAMENT IS THE LARGEST GROUP` · `A MIRROR FOR THE SOUL` · then, large: `EVERY FEELING HAS A PSALM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: choose a psalm for this week. Sit for a moment and ask yourself honestly how you are. Tired? Grateful? Angry? Waiting? Homesick? Then think back over this month's psalms and let one rise that fits. The deer at the dry stream. The very present help. Out of the depths. The weaned child. The new song. Don't pick the one you think you should. Pick the one that sounds like you. Hold it in mind for the rest of the sit. If you pray, you can pray it this week. If you don't, read it once a day as a mirror. The bell holds the time.
Five books of prayers. The Psalms, gathered into five collections, each ending in a blessing, with room for every feeling.

Your line: every feeling has a psalm. This week we went from the depths to a weaned child, Babylon, being knit together, everything praising, and hallelujah. Today, when a strong feeling comes, ask which psalm has already prayed it. Day four hundred forty-one.

howItsDone: Many Christians pray through the whole book of Psalms regularly: monasteries traditionally chant all 150 every week, and the Book of Common Prayer sets them out to be read through every month.

fork.setup: you're editing a book of prayers for a whole people. you have joyful songs, angry songs, sad songs. what do you do with the sad ones?
options: cut them, to keep it uplifting.
put them all at the back.
keep them throughout, more of them than any other kind.
fork.reveal: lament is the largest group of psalms, woven all through the book, right up to its ending in hallelujah.

original.note: Hebrew: praises. the Hebrew name of the book of Psalms, though it is full of laments.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Psalms are a big hymnbook in no special order.
what it means: five collections, gathered over centuries, with a psalm for every feeling.
what a scholar hears: each book ends with a doxology (41:13, 72:18–19, 89:52, 106:48), and 72:20 is a seam left from an earlier collection.

notes: Week-end look-back (days 435–441) in the carry; the hook also looks back over the Psalms block (days 412–440).
'The longest book in the Bible' by chapter count (150). Confirm phrasing.
Midrash Tehillim 1:2: 'Moses gave Israel the five books of the Torah, and David gave Israel the five books of Psalms.' Paraphrased; confirm.

Athanasius, Letter to Marcellinus (ch. 10–12): the Psalms as a mirror; 'speak for you' is a paraphrase of his idea that the reader takes the psalms' words as their own. Confirm the paraphrase is fair.
Calvin's phrase 'an anatomy of all the parts of the soul' (preface to Commentary on the Psalms, 1557), paraphrased, not quoted. Confirm.
Lament as the largest category (Gunkel's form criticism; individual and communal laments together). Confirm.
howItsDone: Rule of St Benedict sets the full Psalter weekly; BCP 1662 monthly cycle. Confirm.
